claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains discrete tungsten and copper phases with sharp, unmodified interfaces.
Controlled carbon addition or tungsten-particle surface treatment during consolidation can form an in-situ WC layer at W/Cu interfaces.
The targeted WC interlayer is less than 100 nm thick and uniformly distributed.
The nanoscale WC layer bridges the tungsten and copper phases.
A WC interlayer lessens the acoustic-impedance mismatch at the W/Cu boundary.
A WC interlayer reduces phonon scattering at the W/Cu boundary.
Reduced acoustic-impedance mismatch and phonon scattering lower W/Cu thermal boundary resistance.
Lower W/Cu thermal boundary resistance increases the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
WC has inherent hardness and chemical stability.
The hardness and chemical stability of WC help maintain interfacial bonding.
Maintained interfacial bonding sustains mechanical strength.
The WC-modified interface resists irradiation-induced damage.
The WC-modified composite is predicted to have approximately 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable composite with unmodified W/Cu interfaces.
The WC-modified composite is predicted to preserve or modestly enhance mechanical durability relative to the unmodified control.
The WC-modified composite is predicted to preserve or modestly enhance irradiation resistance relative to the unmodified control.
The beneficial effects require the WC interlayer to be sufficiently thin and continuous.
An excessively thick or nonuniform carbide layer could reduce ductility or create stress concentrations.
The WC-modified interface must remain stable during thermal cycling and irradiation for the hypothesis to apply to heat-dissipation components and fusion-reactor joints.
